title: Could your team be burying its best ideas?
summary: People are more likely to contribute when they believe they'll be heard rather than judged.
body_markdown:
*At RELX, creating an environment where people feel safe to speak up, share ideas and learn from mistakes is recognised as an important factor in performance, learning and inclusion. I sat down with Penny Newton-Hurley, a specialist trainer in communication skills and psychological safety, to ask about the everyday behaviours that help teams surface risks, learn from mistakes and make room for more voices.*


---


## **What is psychological safety?**


At its simplest, it is a shared belief that you will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with an idea, question, concern or mistake. It does not mean everyone agrees or every suggestion is adopted. The goal is the zone in which we learn: people feel safe enough to contribute and are also expected to challenge, learn and deliver. Safety without accountability can become comfort; accountability without safety can create anxiety.


## **Why is it so closely connected to performance?**


A team cannot use knowledge that people keep to themselves. When colleagues feel able to report problems, ask for help and question assumptions, risks surface earlier and decisions draw on more of the team’s expertise. Strong teams enable people to ask for feedback, try unfamiliar responsibilities, learn from setbacks and develop their contribution – helping drive personal growth. One powerful research example is that in one hospital study, better-performing teams reported more errors - not necessarily because they made more, but because people felt able to report them.


## **What are the signs that a team may not feel safe?**


They are often subtle: meetings run very smoothly, agreement comes quickly, the same people speak, questions are rare and bad news arrives late. You may also see reluctance to ask for help, ideas being dismissed, people being excluded, humour used to belittle mistakes, negative talk behind someone’s back or unnecessary escalation. A quiet team is not necessarily an aligned team – it is a signal to explore. It may be a team whose members are carefully managing how they appear to others.


## **Is creating such an environment mainly a manager’s responsibility?**


Managers have particular influence because their response to a concern or mistake teaches everyone what will happen the next time somebody speaks up - but it belongs to all of us. Leaders can frame the work, invite participation and respond productively. Colleagues can listen, ask questions, share uncertainty, offer help, challenge respectfully and make space for other voices. Everyone contributes to the climate a team creates.


## What practical steps can managers take?


First, ask open questions and allow enough silence for people to think. Try: “What counter-ideas do we have?” or “What are we not considering?”. Second, use conversational turn-taking and consider speaking last, so authority does not unintentionally close down discussion. Third, thank the messenger - even when the message is uncomfortable - and explain what will happen next. People stop contributing when they repeatedly speak up and see no response. Offering written as well as verbal ways to contribute can also help. Managers also need to recognise that openly admitting they do not know things, they make mistakes and are open to feedback is important - it shows humility and gives permission for others to do the same.


## **How can everyone else help?**


Be willing to ask the question others may be avoiding, while linking it to the team’s shared purpose. Admit when you do not know something and ask for help. Listen to understand rather than preparing your reply. Give credit, create space for colleagues who have not yet contributed, without putting anyone under pressure and offer a written route as well. This is not permission to be careless or unkind; candour works best when it is direct, respectful and focused on helping the team succeed.


## **How should teams respond to mistakes and risk-taking?**


Risk-taking is not recklessness. Teams should agree what responsible experimentation looks like and where the boundaries are. When something goes wrong, replace blame with curiosity: what happened, what did we learn and what will we change? A simple recurring agenda item - “What did not go well, and what can we learn from it?” - can make reflection normal rather than threatening. Accountability still matters, but it should help the team move forward rather than make people hide the next problem.


## **What matters in global, matrix, hybrid or cross-functional teams?**


Participation needs to be designed, not assumed. At the start, clarify the purpose, roles, dependencies, unknowns, decision-making and ways to raise things that get in the way of success. Build regular feedback loops and offer different routes for input - during meetings, in writing and one-to-one. Do not confuse confidence, verbal fluency or speed of response with the quality of someone’s contribution. Allow thinking time, check understanding and make it easier for people across cultures, locations and working styles to be heard. For hybrid teams - asynchronous participation, time-zone fairness and the principle that visibility in an office or speed in a live meeting should not determine whose contribution is valued.


## **How does RELX know whether psychological safety is improving?**


Our employee opinion survey helps make the topic concrete. We have questions that explore whether mistakes are held against people; whether tough issues can be raised; whether it is difficult to ask for help; whether risk-taking feels safe; whether difference is rejected; whether people’s unique skills are valued; and whether colleagues undermine one another. This is a starting point, not the conversation itself. Teams should explore what experience sits beneath the findings, choose a behaviour to change and then revisit it.


## **What is one question every team could ask this week?**


**“What have we missed or not considered - and what would make it easier to raise it?”**


The question matters, but the response matters more. Pause. Listen fully. Thank the person. Explore the evidence. Then be clear about what will happen next. A safe environment is built by repeated moments in which people discover that speaking honestly is productive and worthwhile.
